title: The Basic Sentence
intro: This chapter introduces a three-part sentence pattern (the past particle, a preverbal pronoun, the verb) and shows you how to say what someone did and ask whether something happened. The sentence *Sā timu?* ("Did it rain?") is your first example of asking whether something happened.

example.samoan: Sā ʻou alu.

title: Preverbal and Independent Pronouns
intro: So far, two pronouns have filled the slot between the past particle and the verb: *ʻou* (I) and *ia* (he, she). This chapter completes the preverbal pronoun set, every person and three numbers, as in *Sā ʻoutou siva?* ("Did you all dance?"), and introduces the independent pronouns, a second set for the two jobs the preverbal forms cannot do.

example.samoan: Sā lātou alu.

title: Describing Verbs
intro: This chapter expands the past particle + pronoun + verb pattern by adding the verb phrase's two modifier slots, and shows that the words which describe an action are themselves verbs. A describing verb follows the action verb, as in *Sā ʻou foi fiafia* ("I returned happily"); the want word *fia* stands before it, as in *Sā ʻou fia alu* ("I wanted to go").

example.samoan: Sā ʻou foi.

title: The Tense Particles
intro: Building on the past particle *sā*, this chapter completes the tense line by introducing the three remaining tense particles: the second past *na*, for a single finished event; the change particle *ʻua*, for a change that usually leaves a new state in place; and the future particle *ʻoleʻā*.

example.samoan: ʻOleʻā ʻou alu.

title: Commands
intro: This chapter introduces the command: a bare verb with no tense particle in front of it, and shows you how to tell one person to do something.

example.samoan: Nofo.

title: Articles and Plurals
intro: This chapter introduces the article system, the words that stand in front of a noun to mark whether the speaker means one particular thing or just any thing, and whether one or many, and it shows you how to talk about a thing, the thing, and things.
sections: One and Many: The Article Carries the Number

example.samoan: Sā alu le teine.

title: The Naming Sentence
intro: This chapter introduces the naming sentence, a second sentence type that sets two naming parts side by side with the presenting particle *ʻo* and no verb, and shows you how to say who someone is and what something is.

example.samoan: ʻO se uō le tama.

title: Who and What Questions
intro: This chapter introduces the question words of the naming sentence, *ai* ("who") and *ā* ("what"), together with the optional question markers *po* and *ʻea*, and shows you how to ask who someone is and what something is.

example.samoan: ʻO ai ʻoe?

title: Greetings and Courtesy
intro: This chapter gathers the everyday formulas of greeting, thanks, farewell, and good wishes, and shows that each is built on a sentence shape already taught: the tense-particle-free command and exclamation. It also carries the respect vocabulary (*ʻupu faʻaaloalo*) and the everyday speech style for recognition, completing the two speech styles named in the Introduction.

example.samoan: Mānaia le meaʻai!

title: Possessives
intro: This chapter introduces the two belonging words *a* and *o*, which join a thing to the person it belongs to, and the singular possessive forms *laʻu* (my), *lou* (your), *lona* (her), and their partners, and shows you how to speak of my, your, and her things and put real grammar behind the name question met earlier in this book.

example.samoan: ʻO le fale o le aliʻi.

title: Location and Direction
intro: This chapter introduces the place word *i*, which sets an action in a place or sends it toward one, and the from-word *mai*, which marks where something started. The place word stretches a sentence like *Sā ʻou alu* (I went) into *Sā ʻou alu i le nuʻu* (I went to the village), and the from-word answers where a thing came from, as in *Na oso le tama mai le solofanua* (the boy jumped from the horse).

example.samoan: Sā ʻou alu i le nuʻu.

title: Verbs of Wanting and Seeing
intro: This chapter introduces the two-participant sentence: a verb of seeing, feeling, wanting, or asking, then the one who does it, then the thing it reaches, marked by the place word *i*. The pattern points at that thing with the same *i* that sets an action in a place, as in *Sā alofa le tama i le teine* (the boy loved the girl).

example.samoan: Sā vaʻai le teine i le iʻa.

title: The General Particle *E*
intro: This chapter adds the general particle *e*, the tense particle for what holds in general rather than at one moment: a habit, a lasting quality, a plain truth, or something still to come. It is the one tense particle whose shape follows the pronoun, standing as *e* with no pronoun (*E alu le pasi*, the bus goes) and turning into *te* right after one (*ʻOu te alu*, I go).

example.samoan: E malosi le tama.

title: The There-Is Verbs
intro: This chapter adds the two there-is verbs, *iai* (there is) and its built-in negative *leai* (there is none), each a full verb that carries its own tense particle. The same verb *iai* also says what someone has, by saying that the thing exists.

example.samoan: E iai sina vai?

title: The Negative
intro: This chapter adds Samoan's two negative words for the statement: the not-word *lē*, which denies that something happened, and the not-yet word *leʻi*, which says it has not happened so far. Each drops into the slot right after the tense particle and in front of the verb, and the same machinery completes the naming sentence taught earlier in this book, giving Samoan its way to say that something is not so.
sections: Denying a Change, Denying a Habit

example.samoan: Sā siva le teine.

title: The Pointing-Back Word *Ai*
intro: This chapter adds the pointing-back word *ai*, a word that sits inside the verb phrase and stands in for a place already named, so that a place mentioned once does not have to be named a second time. Its companion form *i ai* does the same work for the goal of a movement, the "to there" of going and coming.

example.samoan: Sā nofo le teine i le nuʻu.
example.english: The girl lived in the village.

title: The Where-Sentence
intro: This chapter adds the where-sentence, the third kind of Samoan sentence, in which a tense particle sits in front of a place or a time, standing where a verb would stand, so the sentence says where or when someone or something is. It also teaches the where-question, *ʻO fea...?* ("Where...?"), which runs through the same frame.
sections: The Tense Particle on a Place
The Where-Sentence and the There-Is Verb

example.samoan: Sā i le fale le teine.
example.english: The girl was in the house.

title: Time Words
intro: This chapter adds the time-word slot at the end of the sentence, a set of words such as *ananafi* (yesterday) and *ʻātaeao* (tomorrow morning) that fix a statement to a point in time. The word sits after everything else, and its front end points the same way in time as the tense particle at the start.
sections: Time Past and Time to Come
Words That Stand on Their Own

example.samoan: Na fānau le pepe anapō.
example.english: The baby was born last night.

title: Plural Verb Forms
intro: This chapter adds the plural verb form, the shape a verb takes when what it is about is more than one, so that *nofo* (one person stays) becomes *nonofo* (several stay). The same number appears on describing verbs, reaches plural commands, and settles onto group words such as *aiga* (family).

example.samoan: Sā nofo le teine.

title: The With-Word *Ma*
intro: This chapter adds the with-word *ma*, a single word that joins a companion to an action as "with" and joins two doers as "and". Whether *ma* means "with" or "and" is read from the number of the verb, where the verb has a plural form to show: singular for "with", plural for "and".
sections: The Number of the Verb Tells You Which

example.samoan: Sā fāgota le tama ma le vaʻa.
example.english: The boy went fishing with the canoe.

title: Question Words
intro: This chapter adds the question words of the verb sentence, who, what, where, when, and how, each standing in the place of the thing it asks about. The fact this chapter turns on is that the word for "when" comes in two shapes, one for future time and one for past.

example.samoan: ʻO ai na alu?

title: Numbers, Prices, and Time of Day
intro: This chapter teaches the counting construction: a Samoan number is a kind of verb, so the number of particular things is set after the noun with the general particle *e* (*tama e tolu*, three boys), and the same shape tells the clock hour. It also adds the way to count people and to put things in order.

example.samoan: E tolu tama.

title: Checkpoint 1: The Beginner Consolidation
intro: This checkpoint adds no new grammar. It gathers the whole Beginner band into one place and puts the systems to work together. By now you have built three sentence types, the verb sentence, the naming sentence, and the where-sentence, and with them you can greet, identify, locate, describe, negate, question, count, and command. The exercises and the self-run that follow put those abilities to work together.

example.samoan: Sā ʻou alu.

title: Prohibitions
intro: This chapter adds the two do-not verbs, *ʻaua* and *sōia*, each standing at the head of the sentence in front of the person and verb for what must not be done, so you can tell someone not to do something. A command takes no not-word; to forbid an action, Samoan reaches for a verb of its own.
sections: When More Than One Is Meant

example.samoan: ʻAua ʻe te faʻasāunoa i mea ola.

title: The Possessive System in Full
intro: This chapter completes the two belonging words *a* and *o*, adding the rule of control that decides between them, the four sets of possessive forms that track the articles across one thing and many, and the owners that come in pairs and groups, and the for-word *mo*, so you can speak of anyone's things in any number and say who a thing is for. Where the control rule runs out, a word's belonging type is a fact of that word, and this chapter gives the lists.
sections: The Four Sets of Possessive Forms

example.samoan: ʻO le leitiō a le aliʻi.

title: Spatial Nouns
intro: This chapter adds the spatial nouns, the closed set of words that name the regions around a thing, its inside, its top, its back, together with the words for the compass points and for the seaward and inland directions. It fits them into a frame built from the place word *i* and the belonging word *o*, both already taught, so you can say where one thing sits in relation to another.

example.samoan: ʻO le laau i tua o le fale.

title: The Agent Marker *E*
intro: This chapter adds the agent marker *e*, the word that sets apart the doer in a sentence with two participants, and shows you how to say who did what to whom. It also teaches what Samoan does in place of an English passive, which is to leave the doer out and put nothing where it stood.
sections: Verbs That Take a Doer, and Verbs That Do Not

example.samoan: Sā fafaga e le tama le moa.

title: The Maker-Prefix *Faʻa-*
intro: This chapter introduces the maker-prefix *faʻa-*, which stands in front of a noun or a verb and builds a new word out of it, and shows you how to read a built word by reading the word standing inside it. It is the most common prefix in Samoan, and the word it builds is usually a verb.

example.samoan: Sā faʻamoe e le teine le pepe.
example.english: The girl put the baby to sleep.

title: Directional Particles
intro: This chapter introduces the direction words, the six particles that stand after a verb and say which way its action is turned, toward the speaker, away from the speaker, up, down, along or away, and shows you how to orient an action in space relative to yourself and the person you are speaking to. The same words also stand inside a spatial noun, as in *i lalo ifo o le fale* (underneath the house).
sections: A Direction Word Inside a Spatial Noun

example.samoan: Faʻatali mai.

title: The Complement Clause: Can and Must
intro: This chapter introduces the complement clause, a whole clause that stands where a noun phrase would otherwise stand, and the one word that opens it, *ona* (that). The words that take such a clause are the ability and obligation words *mafai* (can) and *tatau* (must), so you can say what people can, must, and should do.
sections: The Words That Take a Complement Clause
When the Second Verb Keeps Its Own Tense

example.samoan: E sā ona ulaula.

title: Comparison and Degree
intro: This chapter adds the comparison patterns: the direction word *atu* carrying the comparative degree, the than-word *i lo* naming what a thing is measured against, and the verbs *sili* (best), *pei* (like) and *tusa* (the same). The quality word keeps its shape in every pattern here, so these separate words carry the whole job, and with them you can say that one thing has more of a quality than another, that one thing stands above the rest, and that two things are alike.
sections: Naming What You Compare With: *I Lo*
Saying Two Things Are Alike: *Pei* and *Tusa Ma*

example.samoan: E malosi atu le tama.

title: Short and Long Verb Forms
intro: This chapter introduces the long form of the verb, a second shape that verbs taking the agent marker carry beside the plain one, and shows you how to build it and the two places where the choice is settled for you.
sections: The Two Shapes of the Verb
Commands: The Two Rules That Hold

example.samoan: Sā fasi le tama e le teine.

title: Reported Speech
intro: This chapter adds reported speech, which Samoan builds from machinery already in place: after a knowing or ordering word the report is an ordinary clause keeping a tense particle of its own, and after the say-verb *fai* it is a sentence of its own. Reading that particle against the time the first half names, not against the moment of speaking, is the one new rule, and it is what lets you pass on anything anyone said, asked, ordered or knew.
sections: The Tense Particle Inside the Report

example.samoan: ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻua sau le teine.
example.english: The boy knows that the girl has come.

title: Putting Things First
intro: This chapter teaches putting things first, the pattern that moves a noun phrase out of its ordinary place to the head of the sentence under the presenting particle *ʻo*, and shows you how to mark a topic, draw a contrast, put weight on one word, or say where and when. The shape of the verb and the pointing-back word *ai* both answer to that move.
sections: Moving the Doer to the Front
Only and Any at the Front
The Four Jobs of Putting Things First

example.samoan: Sā gālue le tama i le faʻatoʻaga.
example.english: The boy worked in the plantation.

title: The Le-Phrase
intro: This chapter introduces the le-phrase, an article standing in front of a verb so that the two of them together work as a noun phrase, and shows you how to pack a whole event into a thing you can put wherever a noun phrase goes.

example.samoan: ʻOu te lē fia manatu i le mea lea.
example.english: I do not want to think about that.

title: Conjunctions
intro: This chapter adds the words that join two whole clauses, *ma* (and), *ʻae* (but) and *ʻaʻo* (while), together with the rule that settles the tense particle of the second clause, and shows you how to build one sentence out of two.

example.samoan: Sā timu ma sā lolo le vai.
example.english: It rained and the water overflowed.

title: Narrative Chains
intro: This chapter adds two of the ways Samoan sets one event after another, the then-construction built out of *ona* and *lea* and the run of clauses that carry no tense particle of their own, and shows you how to tell a story in the order its events happened.
sections: The Shorter Shapes of the Then-Construction

example.samoan: Ona alu lea ʻo le tama.

title: Purpose and Reason
intro: This chapter adds the three because-words *ʻauā*, *leaga* and *ʻona*, each of which opens a clause giving the reason for what was just said, and the purpose clause, which says what an action is done for. It also teaches the why-question, so you can ask for a reason as well as give one.

example.samoan: Sā taatia le teine i le fale ʻauā ʻua vaivai.
example.english: The girl lay down in the house because she was tired.

title: Conditionals and When-Clauses
intro: This chapter adds the condition clause, which says what has to be true before the rest of the sentence can happen, and teaches its two shapes: the one opened by the if-word *ʻāfai*, and the one that opens with the short form of the future particle and no joining word at all. It also shows where the condition clause stands when it comes after the main clause instead of in front of it, so you can say what depends on what in either order.
sections: The Tense Particle in a Condition Clause
The Condition Clause Without a Joining Word

example.samoan: ʻĀfai e timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.
example.english: If it rains tomorrow, the trip will not go.

title: Modifiers in Depth
intro: This chapter takes the describing verb into the noun phrase, where it stands after the name of a thing instead of after an action, and adds the two compound shapes that fill the same position, so you can pack a whole description into one noun phrase. It also shows what happens when several describing verbs stand on one noun, and where the pointing word goes when they do.
sections: The Describing Verb After a Noun
Plural Describing Verbs After a Noun

example.samoan: E uliuli le taʻavale.

title: Checkpoint 2: The Intermediate Consolidation
intro: This chapter adds no new grammar and no new words, and consolidates the Intermediate band, from the do-not verbs and the agent marker to the condition clause and the describing verb inside a noun phrase. It sets those systems to work in the same sentences through mixed exercises and a closing self-run, and shows you how to narrate, argue, compare, report and explain with agent marking and clause combining running together.
sections: Joining Clauses and Telling What Happened Next

example.samoan: Sā tatala e le teine le pusa.

title: The Belonging Sentence
intro: This chapter adds the belonging-sentence, in which a tense particle sits in front of an owner joined to a belonging word, so the sentence says who a thing belongs to. It also completes the whose-question, *ʻO ai...?* ("Whose...?"), which runs through the same frame.

example.samoan: E a mātou le taʻavale.

title: Relative Clauses
intro: This chapter introduces the describing clause, a clause with a tense particle of its own standing behind a noun and saying which person, thing, place, or time is meant. It adds the one-who word *ē* and the pointing-back word inside the clause, and shows you how to build the person who left and the village you stayed in.
sections: The Two Ways the Missing Word Is Shown
When the Doer Is the Missing Word
The Thing It Was Done With, and the Thing It Was Aimed At

example.samoan: ʻO le fafine sā alu i le nuʻu.
example.english: The woman who went to the village.

title: Time Expressions
intro: This chapter completes the time-expression system with the since-word *talu* and the clause that follows it, the when-word *ina ʻua*, the le-phrase set at the head of a sentence as a way to set the time in a story, and the ways Samoan says how often. It shows you how to place a whole episode in time, from *talu ona ʻou sau* (since I came) to *i taeao o aso taʻi=tasi* (every morning).
sections: The Le-Phrase at the Head of a Sentence

example.samoan: Talu ona ʻou sau ʻou te leʻi maua se mea lelei.
example.english: Since I came, I have not got anything good.

title: The Le-Phrase in Full
intro: This chapter completes the le-phrase by adding the people and things its event involves, and shows you how to say whose crying, whose feeding, and who fed whom. The belonging words *a* and *o* do that naming, and inside a le-phrase they answer to a rule of their own.
sections: The One the Event Is About
When the Choice Is Made for You
The Thing the Event Happens To

example.samoan: ʻO le taliga o le tama.

title: Uses of the Le-Phrase
intro: This chapter teaches three uses of the le-phrase: after the with-word *ma*, after a verb that passes judgement such as *lelei* (good), and standing on its own as an exclamation. It shows you how to say what state someone is in while acting, how to pass judgement on an event, and how to comment on the way someone is reacting.

example.samoan: Sā ʻou nofo ma le lē fiafia.

title: Word Class Flexibility
intro: This chapter completes the principle set out in the Introduction as the slot rule, under which a word such as *uō* (friend) is a verb when it fills the verb slot of a sentence and a noun when it fills a noun slot. It also sorts the nouns that rule produces into five kinds, and shows you how to read a word's class from its slot and why a name that refers to people takes the place word *iā*.

example.samoan: E alofa le tama i le teine.

title: The Mood Particles
intro: This chapter completes the tense particles with the four mood particles, polite-command *ʻia*, wish-and-permission *seʻi*, until *seʻia* and warning *neʻi*, which stand where a tense particle stands, and shows you how to make a polite command, ask permission, make a wish, say until when, and warn against what should not happen.

example.samoan: ʻIa tātou onosaʻi.

title: Counterfactuals and Concessives
intro: This chapter completes the condition clause with the second if-word, *ʻana*, which opens a condition that did not come true, and shows you how to say what would have happened. It also adds *seʻiloga* (unless) and the sentences built on the verbs *ui* (granted), *tīgā* (painful) and *tusa* (the same), which say that one thing holds in spite of another.
sections: Even If, Whether or Not, and Whatever with *Tusa*

example.samoan: ʻĀfai ʻe te lē sau, ʻou te alu atu.
example.english: If you do not come, I will go and see you.

title: Affixes and Doubling
intro: This chapter completes Samoan's word-building system, the two endings *=ga* and *=a*, the prefixes *fe-*, *taʻi-*, *toʻa-*, *ʻā-* and *ana-*, and the doubling of a word or of a piece of one, and shows you how to read a built word you have never met. Many of the plural forms learned one at a time earlier in this book are made by that doubling, and this chapter names the process behind them.
sections: Doubling a Piece of the Word
Number in the Colour and Size Words
What a Doubled Word Can Carry

example.samoan: Sā nonofo teine.

title: Emotional Articles and Pronouns
intro: This chapter completes the article system with the four articles that carry feeling, *si*, *sina*, *nāi* and *ni nāi*, and completes the first person with its emotional forms, *ʻita*, *taʻita* and the middle-slot *ta*. Together they mark sympathy, an amount presented as modest, humility, and an appeal for help.

example.samoan: Sau si aʻu tama.
